Guide to the FY 2027 – FY 2032
Adopted Capital Improvement
Program
The Capital Improvement Program (CIP) is one of the definitive products of the County’s
process for forecasting and planning its future capital facility growth, in conjunction with
department service plans, the Capital Needs Assessment, and the 2019 Comprehensive Plan.
This planning process addresses the County’s projected capital needs associated with new
development together with the CIP funding plan and budget.
The CIP provides a six-year forecast of the County Government and School Division’s
land, facility, and equipment needs, with a financing plan to implement each need. The CIP
plans for the land acquisition, design, construction, and capital equipment procurement for
each project. Potential projects are evaluated in relation to each other and compared to
articulated Board and department priorities to ensure that the highest priority projects
receive funding, with essential improvements planned in a manner commensurate with the
County’s ability to pay.
The CIP is developed biennially, with the six-year period moving out an additional two
years every other fiscal year. The FY 2027 budget process represents the start of a new
biennial period, FY 2027 through FY 2032. The CIP is a multi-year plan that does not
constitute or require appropriation of funds beyond those for the adopted fiscal year, FY
2027. The FY 2028 - FY 2032 period includes projects with planned funding that should be
considered for future appropriations in subsequent budgets. Funding decisions concerning
the CIP are made in combination with decisions regarding the County’s operating budget, as
the two are critically related. Final authority to spend funds for purposes specified in the
County’s operating and capital budgets is accomplished through the adoption of an
Appropriations Resolution by the Board of Supervisors.
The FY 2027 Adopted CIP abides by all County fiscal policies and debt ratios. Projects
approved for FY 2027 will receive funding appropriations as part of the Adopted Budget;
projects proposed for the FY 2028 - FY 2032 period provide only planned appropriations
and are subject to change in subsequent budget development cycles.

Concepts
Structure of the CIP
The CIP is divided into five sections: CIP Overview, Previously Authorized and Future Projects,
County Projects, Transportation Projects, and School Projects. Project pages provide
pertinent information in an easy-to-read format.

This section provides a general overview of projects that had prior year funding that are still
considered “active” and projects that would be considered for funding prioritization in future
capital budget processes, or “Future Fiscal Years.”

Projects
The capital projects in the CIP are organized into three categories: County Projects,
Transportation Projects, and School Projects.

County Projects
Administration includes land acquisition funds, general contingency, and staffing and
contractual support. Most projects support the administration and management of the CIP.
General Government includes general capital projects such as government offices,
warehouses, support space, storm water management, projects at the County Landfill, and
the County’s Renovation Program. Most projects are associated with and managed by the
Department of General Services and/or the Department of Transportation and Capital
Infrastructure.
Health and Welfare includes capital projects for the County’s human service agencies.
Most projects are managed by the Department of Transportation and Capital Infrastructure.
Information Technology encompasses all information technology systems acquisition and
implementation projects. Most projects are associated with and managed by the
Department of Information Technology.
Parks, Recreation, and Culture includes recreational capital projects such as libraries,
parks, recreation centers, community centers, and senior centers. The section also includes
a renovation program specifically for use by the Department of Parks, Recreation, and
Community Services to maintain its assets, including fields. Most projects are managed by
the Department of Transportation and Capital Infrastructure.
Public Safety includes capital projects in support of the County’s public safety facilities (not
systems). Most projects are managed by the Department of Transportation and Capital
Infrastructure.
Towns projects include all capital projects for which the County contributes funds to
incorporated towns.

Transportation Projects
These projects include planning, preliminary engineering, right-of-way acquisition, utility
relocation, and construction of roads, interchanges, roundabouts, intersection
improvements, trails, sidewalks, traffic signals, and park and ride lots. The transit projects
include bus shelter and bus stop construction, the procurement of transit buses, and the
Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority (WMATA) metro contribution subsidy. The
Transportation section of the document is divided into the following programs: intersection
improvement program, road projects; sidewalks and trails projects; and transit projects.

School Projects
These projects include design and construction funding for Loudoun County Public Schools
(LCPS). The LCPS CIP is adopted by the School Board and recommended for approval by the
Board of Supervisors. The School Projects section of the document is divided into the
following programs: elementary schools, middle schools, high schools, and other school
projects.

Local Tax Funding
The Board of Supervisors’ fiscal policy establishes a goal of 10 percent “pay-as-you-go” cash
funding in the CIP. This 10 percent cash funding can be comprised of local tax funding, which

Capital Projects Fund on transportation projects; prior to FY 2022 this amount had roughly
equated to two cents of the real property tax rate but has been higher since FY 2023. Two
cents of the real property tax rate remains committed to transportation projects in FY 2027. A
detailed description of the County’s requirements related to the Northern Virginia

Factors Affecting the FY 2027 – FY

CIP Development Criteria
The CIP development process includes evaluating the funding needs of existing projects and
the ability to add new projects based on the estimated available revenue and debt capacity.
New projects can include projects that were previously identified as priorities for future year
funding that would move into the six-year period, or projects that have come up off-cycle that
the Board collectively has directed staff to include in the CIP. The Board has typically
confirmed for staff to follow a general set of criteria for capital budget development,
including but not limited to: address existing and recurring projects budgets before adding
new projects, add new projects in the later years of the CIP, maximize and leverage the use of
non-local revenue sources, especially for transportation projects, and Town projects should
only be considered after County and School projects have been accommodated.
Additionally, the Board has consistently adopted capital budgets that generally allocate
available revenue with 30 percent to County projects, 30 percent to School Division projects,
and 40 percent to Transportation projects.

In July 2025, the Board provided guidance for the FY 2027 Adopted CIP that included more
specific criteria as a basis for evaluating and recommending new projects to enter the CIP.
This criterion includes highest priority being given to projects aligned with policy documents;
including the Capital Needs Assessment (CNA), Countywide Transportation Plan (CTP), and
general government Space Strategy, and the Board’s strategic initiatives, and projects that
address health and safety issues, followed by other factors such as sustainability, equity,
overall customer impact; and for transportation projects, continuation of current corridor
improvements and a project’s dependence on improvements outside of Loudoun County to
achieve a benefit.

Board Priorities and Policy-Driven Projects
The new six-year period, in which two new years are added, allows the Board to make further
progress with its capital budget priorities. Cost increases and schedule adjustments for
existing projects are addressed before new projects are added. The Adopted CIP includes a
significant cost increase of $108 million for the Western Loudoun Recreation Complex to
develop the project as originally scoped. Policy-driven projects identified in the CNA have
been added to the later years of the CIP for planning and development. This includes a
strategy for addressing library square footage in Eastern Loudoun County, a District Park and
other parkland acreage, and Group Homes for the Department of Mental Health, Substance
Abuse and Developmental Services. The Adopted CIP also provides funding for the design
and construction of a new headquarters and fleet maintenance facility in FY 2027 for the
Department of General Services (DGS) which was initially planned to be acquired through a
lease-purchase arrangement associated with a legislative application. The legislative
application was deferred indefinitely by the applicant at the October 7, 2025, Board Business

Local Tax Funding and Annual Debt Issuance Guideline Adjustments
In July 2025, the Board provided guidance in support of an increase to the Annual Debt
Issuance Guideline (ADIG) for CIP planning and development. The new ADIG was set at $525
million for FY 2027, $575 million FY 2028, $625 million for FY 2029, $675 million for FY 2030
and $725 million for FY 2031-2032. Subsequent to this CIP guidance, the Board provided
budget development guidance that included sending 80 percent of the “excess” local tax
funding (LTF) revenue above the target operating budget growth rates of 9 percent for the
County and 8 percent for Loudoun County Public Schools to the CIP, with the remaining 20
percent going to the Housing Fund. The intent of this action was to use more LTF rather than
taking advantage of the full ADIG to not significantly expand the CIP, and also to reserve debt
capacity for later years when less LTF is projected to be available. As a result, each year of
the CIP retains debt issuance capacity under the ADIG. Local tax funding and debt financing
make up 29 percent and 56 percent of the total six-year period funding, respectively.

School Board’s Adopted CIP
The School Board’s adopted CIP is fully accommodated for the six-year plan. The CIP reflects
an expectation that no new schools will be needed within the next six and possibly ten years
to accommodate growth in the school system, so an elementary school previously planned in
the CIP, ES-36, has been moved out of the six-year period. Most of the funding in the School
Board’s adopted CIP is in Capital Renewal and Alteration (CRA), which provides funding
annually to replace, repair, and update critical facility systems; renovate and/or renew
buildings; and/or install needed technology upgrades.

Project Cost Changes and Cost Estimation Methodology
As part of the annual CIP development process, staff reviews and updates cost estimation
methodologies, including assumptions for inflation over the project’s duration and
determining the appropriate contingency levels. Initial cost estimates are based on historical
data, with adjustments made for any unique project characteristics. At the early stages of
development, the costs of land acquisition, design, and furniture, fixtures and equipment are
typically calculated as a percentage of the “hard” costs. These estimates are refined as the
project approaches its first year of appropriation. During the project’s planning phase, before
design or engineering begins, cost estimates are highly uncertain and can range from 50
percent below to 200 percent above the final project cost. Accuracy improves significantly
once the design phase is underway, with consultants playing a key role in developing and
refining cost estimates for both new and existing projects. For the development of the FY
2027 Adopted CIP, staff re-estimated projects in the capital budget based on the following
parameters.

1. Project Re-Estimation
•  Projects were re-estimated if the existing estimates were two or more years old
or if the project reached a significant milestone by the summer of 2025, such
as:
a. Receiving updated cost estimates from design consultants at key
design stages (e.g., 30%, 60%, or 90% design milestones for roads, or
35%, 65%, or 95% milestones for facilities), prompting a reassessment
of initial estimates.
2. Inflation Estimation Updates
•  During the FY 2027 budget development process, staff collaborated with the
Capital Projects Program Management Office to determine that the escalators
applied to previously estimated projects remained sufficient for those projects
and are generally set to three percent in FY 2027 and subsequent years.
•For newly re-estimated projects, planning contingencies were incorporated to
account for price fluctuations. These adjustments will continue to be monitored
in future budget cycles.
3. Planning Contingency Review
•  Planning contingency – allocated amounts to address uncertainty within each
project phase were carefully reviewed. Contingency levels, which typically
decrease as projects advance were adjusted where necessary to reflect
changes in scope or uncertainty.
• Some project budgets were revised upward or downward based on updated
assessments of risk and progress.
Outcomes of the Re-Estimation Process
The re-estimation effort resulted in higher overall costs for projects, limiting the ability to add
new projects within the six-year period. To address these challenges, staff continue to focus
on leveraging additional revenue sources, including:

Staff and Contractual Support for County Projects
The FY 2027 Adopted CIP incorporates County staffing and professional management
consulting costs related to the development, implementation, and monitoring of the CIP
project schedules and budgets. For County staff who work directly on projects, such as
design engineers, land acquisition managers, project managers, and construction/civil
engineers, expenditures are funded through individual project budgets, thereby more
accurately reflecting the true cost of a project. Support positions, including staff who provide
more indirect or general CIP support such as budgeting or procurement, are budgeted
through a central project. The costs of the County’s program management consultants
(discussed below) are also directly charged to project budgets. Direct staffing, support
positions, and program management charges for FY 2027 total $25.8 million.
A contract for program management contractual support began in 2020 to assist in
capital project scheduling, project development performance, engineering support, design
quality assurance, project oversight (including cost estimating), and providing general staff
augmentation to meet schedule and budget goals. As with direct staff costs, the cost of the
program management contract is budgeted in individual capital project budgets.

The FY 2027 Adopted Budget represents the start of a new biennial period, FY 2027 through
FY 2032. There are changes to existing projects and new projects have been added. This
section provides a summary, by election district, of the new projects that were added, and a
summary of changes made during the FY 2027 budget development process, including
updates to project development schedules, material scope changes, and significant budget
changes. Additionally, this section identifies the requestor for each change and outlines
specific project duration changes.

The following terms are used in this section to describe project changes:

Acceleration - indicates a project will be completed sooner due to funding and project
commencement being earlier than previously planned, or that a development phase was
completed earlier than anticipated.

Budget – indicates a project has experienced a material change in cost. This can be
associated with a scope change or an updated cost estimate.

Deferral – indicates a project no longer appears in the six-year period. This is typically
associated with moving a project out of the six-year period to accommodate another project.

Delay - refers to a later completion date than originally planned that is not necessarily
associated with other phasing changes.

Phasing - denotes shifts in development stages such as design, land acquisition, or
construction, which may result in the acceleration or delay of a project’s completion.

Operating Impact Analysis
The costs associated with opening and operating new or renovated facilities are a factor in
calculating the total impact of a capital project. During the Capital Improvement Program
(CIP) budget development process, personnel (FTE), operating, utility, and maintenance
needs are identified based on the specific type of facility and the services that will be
provided. Estimated recurring operating costs, such as personnel and maintenance contracts,
and initial one-time costs, such as computer equipment, training, and uniforms are identified,
and cost estimates are developed. To provide a greater level of accuracy in estimating future
costs, personnel costs were escalated by three percent and operating costs by three percent.
The operating impacts analysis table displays the estimated operating impacts related to
a capital project that is anticipated to open or be completed during the six-year CIP period.
The table provides an analysis of:
•  The number and cost of personnel required to staff new or expanded facilities.
•  Recurring operating costs and one-time opening costs related to a new or
expanded facility, which includes utility and maintenance costs for both the
program department and the centralized internal maintenance or services costs
that will be provided by the Department of General Services and the Department
of Information Technology.
• Annual debt service payments related to the capital project (as applicable).
The Operating Impact Analysis table provides summary-level information that includes
the estimated impact of staffing and operating a new facility, and the incremental increase
above current staffing levels and operations for a facility that was renovated or expanded.
The estimated number of new personnel required to operate a facility is shown in the year in
which the personnel are projected to be hired. In some cases, such as public safety,
personnel may be hired a year before the facility’s opening date to complete required
training, set up operations, and complete necessary pre-opening activities. However, the
summary table does not include additional personnel that may be needed to centrally
manage an expanding County facility inventory by the Department of General Services
(DGS). For example, a Maintenance Technician is requested by DGS for every new 45,000
square feet added to the County to ensure the continuity of service level for preventative
maintenance across all County facilities.
County capital projects that have an operating impact will have an operating impacts
table in their respective CIP budget document page, which lists the project’s estimated
operating, personnel, and debt service costs. In addition, department pages present
projected amounts for capital facilities opening in FY 2027. Project pages for school projects
only include the debt service costs.

Notice of Intent
Notice evidencing the intent to reimburse certain capital improvements expenditures incurred
in anticipation of financing such costs with the issuance of bonds pursuant to Income Tax
Regulation Section 1.150-2 (the “Reimbursement Regulations”):

The Board of Supervisors of the County of Loudoun, Virginia (the “County”), has determined in
connection with adoption of the County’s Fiscal Year 2027 Budget that it is necessary and
desirable to undertake certain capital improvements consisting of the projects and estimated
costs described in the Fiscal Year 2027 Budget with financing as indicated on the Schedule of
Major Financings — Fiscal Years 2027 – 2032 in the maximum amount of $3,147,148,508.
This schedule is provided for convenience in this section and in the Debt Service Fund Section
of this document.

Statement of Intent. The County presently intends, at one time or from time to time, to finance
the indicated projects with either tax-exempt or taxable bonds (the "Bonds") and to reimburse
itself, if needed, under the Reimbursement Regulations, for capital expenditures paid by the
County (including expenditures previously paid by the County to the extent permitted by law)
for the projects with its own funds prior to the date the Bonds are issued. The County intends
that adoption of this Notice as part of the adoption of the Fiscal Year 2027 Budget be
considered as “official intent” within the meaning of the Reimbursement Regulations
promulgated under the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, as amended.

Effective Date. This intent shall be in full force and effect with adoption of the Fiscal Year 2027
Budget and shall apply to all projects described in the Fiscal Year 2027 Budget and the
Schedule of Major Financings – Fiscal Years 2027 – 2032 as of the date of adoption thereof, as
well as any projects added as part of any amendments thereto.

Public Inspection. The Office Director of the Office of Management and Budget shall keep
this intent continuously available for inspection by the general public during the County's
normal business hours.
